The all-time closing high of the S&P500 is $7,818.93. Today it closed at $6,910.39, representing a loss of 11.6% from its all-time high.
I remember an article by Jonathan where he admitted to increasing his stock purchases during broad market declines, something critics would call market timing. He argued against this being true market timing, saying, "I’m not making a big all-or-nothing bet based on a market forecast, but rather responding to what the market has already done."
I've engaged in this same "sinful" behavior over the past few days. Luckily, my purchase decisions were made with a clearer head, prior to these declines, where I set up automatic sell orders from my short and ultra short-term bond funds, contingent upon the S&P500 declining from all-time highs to certain price levels (i.e. 5% down, 7.5% down, 10% down, etc.) Thus I have purchased stocks on sale and according to the predefined rules of my investment plan.
In another article, Jonathan explains his "loosey goosey" strategy for when to rebalance back to his target bond allocation. I've chosen a bit more structure here, choosing to rebalance back into bonds once stocks recover to their all-time highs.
Is this strategy for everyone? Probably not. But for me, I feel the risk is low given that I have no immediate need for the short-term bonds I've used to purchase these discounted stocks. Purchasing stocks on sale also eases the psychological pain of the wider losses of my much larger stock portfolio.
I'm curious how others view this topic, and, if it's something you do, what are your index decline triggers (% from all-time high) for purchasing extra stocks, and when do you rebalance back into bonds. Or, is it all a little loosey goosey?
